overview: The image is visually closest to the normal-cat class in the training taxonomy. This is not a certificate of health: mild, early, hidden or poorly photographed skin disease can be missed by a single image. Use this result as a low-alert visual triage label, especially if the cat has no itching, hair loss, discharge, odor or behavior change.
typical_signs: No obvious focal lesion in the uploaded view
Coat and skin appear broadly even in the photographed area
No visible crusting, circular hair loss, swelling or discharge
No obvious self-trauma such as scratching wounds or overgroomed patches
Image quality, coat color, dirt, grooming and lighting can still hide subtle change
transmission: Normal skin is not a transmissible disease label. If itching, crusting, hair loss or household spread is present, contagious causes such as mites or ringworm still need veterinary consideration even when the image is classified as normal.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether the photographed area looks normal for this cat in the context of the history
Ask whether clearer close-up and wider-view photos would help if signs are subtle
Ask whether an in-person examination is needed if itching, hair loss, odor, discharge or behavior change is present
Ask what changes should be monitored before rechecking the skin
urgent_flags: Pain or strong reaction when the area is touched
Bleeding, open wounds or discharge
Rapid swelling or fast spread of skin changes
Fever, poor appetite, lethargy or hiding behavior
Eye involvement or lesions near the eye
Human skin irritation after contact with the animal

overview: This label means the uploaded dog image is visually closest to the dermatitis examples in the training taxonomy. Dermatitis is a descriptive skin-inflammation category, not a single cause; allergy, parasites, bacterial or yeast overgrowth, irritants, moisture and self-trauma can look similar in photographs. The useful next step is to identify the underlying cause with veterinary examination and, when needed, targeted diagnostic tests.
typical_signs: Red or inflamed skin
Itching, licking, chewing or rubbing
Hair loss around the affected area
Crusting, scaling, scabs or thickened skin
Moist or irritated patches
Odor, debris or discharge when secondary infection is present
Recurrent flares in the same body regions
transmission: Dermatitis itself is a visual description and is not automatically contagious. Transmission risk depends on the cause; parasites, dermatophytes and some infections can spread, while allergic or irritant dermatitis is not contagious.
ask_your_vet: Ask which causes should be ruled out first, such as parasites, infection, allergy or irritant exposure
Ask whether skin cytology, scraping, fungal testing or other diagnostics are appropriate
Ask what history details are useful, including itch pattern, seasonality, diet, flea exposure and contact with other animals
Ask whether other animals or people in the household should be checked if lesions are spreading
urgent_flags: Severe pain, intense itching or inability to rest
Rapidly spreading redness, swelling or skin damage
Pus, bad odor, wet discharge or large open sores
Fever, lethargy, poor appetite or weakness
Lesions involving the face, eye, ear canal, feet or genital region
Multiple animals or people developing skin signs

overview: The image is visually closest to the normal-dog class in the training taxonomy. This does not rule out early, hidden or non-photographed disease, especially if the dog is itchy, painful, smelly, losing hair or behaving differently. Treat this output as a low-alert image finding rather than a medical diagnosis.
typical_signs: No obvious focal lesion in the uploaded view
Skin and coat appear broadly even in the photographed area
No visible open wound, swelling, crusting or discharge
No obvious circular hair loss or moist inflamed patch
Coat density, lighting, motion blur and image angle can obscure mild disease
transmission: Normal skin is not a transmissible disease label. If skin signs are present in other animals or people, or if there is progressive itching or hair loss, contagious causes still need veterinary consideration.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether the photographed area looks normal for this dog given the symptoms and history
Ask whether a clearer close-up, wider body photo or in-person examination is needed
Ask what signs would justify rechecking the skin even if the image looks normal
Ask whether ears, paws, belly or hidden skin folds should also be examined
urgent_flags: Pain, bleeding, open wounds or discharge
Rapid swelling or fast spread of skin changes
Fever, poor appetite, lethargy or weakness
Eye involvement, closed eye or facial swelling
Sudden severe itching or self-injury
Pale gums, collapse or sudden behavior change

overview: The image is visually closest to the ear-mite-in-cat label. Ear mites are a common cause of ear irritation in cats, but waxy debris, bacterial or yeast ear disease, foreign material and skin allergy can produce overlapping signs. A photo cannot confirm mites; veterinary ear examination and microscopic evaluation may be needed.
typical_signs: Ear scratching or rubbing
Head shaking
Dark crumbly ear debris
Redness around the ear or ear flap
Hair loss, crusting or scratches near the ear
Sensitivity when the ear is touched
One or both ears may appear affected
transmission: Ear mites can spread between animals through close contact, especially among cats and other household pets. People are not the usual host, but household spread among animals is important to discuss with a veterinarian.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether otoscopic ear examination or microscopy is needed to confirm mites
Ask whether bacterial, yeast or allergic ear disease should also be considered
Ask whether other cats, dogs or close-contact animals should be checked
Ask what signs would indicate deeper ear involvement or pain
urgent_flags: Head tilt, circling, loss of balance or unusual eye movement
Severe pain or strong resistance to ear handling
Bleeding, swelling or wounds around the ear
Bad odor, heavy discharge or rapidly worsening debris
Loss of appetite, fever or marked lethargy
Sudden hearing or behavior changes

overview: The image is visually closest to the cat eye-infection label. Redness, discharge and swelling around the eye may come from infection, trauma, foreign material, corneal disease, eyelid disease or systemic illness, and these causes cannot be separated reliably from an image alone. Eye problems deserve careful triage because discomfort or vision risk can progress quickly.
typical_signs: Redness around the eye or conjunctiva
Watery, mucus-like or colored discharge
Squinting or holding the eye partly closed
Swelling of eyelids or tissue around the eye
Rubbing the face or pawing at the eye
Cloudiness, surface change or visible irritation
One or both eyes may be affected
transmission: Some infectious eye conditions can spread between cats, but image appearance alone cannot identify the cause. Hygiene and separation questions should be handled through veterinary guidance, especially in multi-cat homes.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether the eye should be examined urgently
Ask what signs suggest pain, corneal injury or vision risk
Ask whether other cats in the household should be checked if signs are spreading
Ask whether the eye, eyelids and surrounding skin need separate evaluation
urgent_flags: Squinting, closed eye or obvious eye pain
Cloudy eye, blue-white haze or visible surface defect
Visible trauma, bleeding or foreign material
Sudden swelling around the eye or face
Apparent vision change, bumping into objects or disorientation
Fever, poor appetite or marked lethargy

overview: The image is visually closest to the dog eye-infection label. Red eye, discharge, swelling and squinting can reflect infection, allergy, trauma, foreign material, corneal ulceration, eyelid disease or other eye disorders. A single image should be used for triage only because some eye conditions require prompt veterinary assessment to protect comfort and vision.
typical_signs: Redness around the eye or conjunctiva
Watery, mucus-like or colored discharge
Squinting or keeping the eye partly closed
Swelling of eyelids or surrounding tissue
Rubbing the face or pawing at the eye
Cloudiness, surface irregularity or visible irritation
Light sensitivity or reluctance to open the eye
transmission: Transmission depends on the underlying cause and cannot be confirmed from a photo. Some infectious causes may spread between animals, while allergy, injury or foreign material are not contagious.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether an eye examination is needed urgently
Ask what signs suggest pain, corneal injury or vision risk
Ask whether discharge is more consistent with infection, irritation, allergy or injury
Ask whether both eyes and the surrounding skin should be evaluated
urgent_flags: Squinting, closed eye or strong light sensitivity
Cloudy eye, blue-white haze or visible injury
Sudden swelling around the eye or face
Apparent vision change or bumping into objects
Bleeding, foreign material or severe discharge
Fever, lethargy or poor appetite

overview: This cattle label means the image is visually closest to foot-and-mouth-disease examples in the dataset. Foot-and-mouth disease is a high-consequence vesicular livestock disease, and similar mouth or foot lesions can have major herd-health and regulatory implications. A suspected case should be handled as a veterinary and animal-health-authority matter rather than a routine skin problem.
typical_signs: Blisters, erosions or ulcers around the mouth, muzzle, tongue, teats or feet
Drooling or difficulty eating
Lameness or reluctance to stand or walk
Fever, dullness or reduced appetite
Reduced milk production in dairy animals
Several animals affected over a short period
Young animals may appear weak or severely unwell
transmission: Foot-and-mouth disease can spread rapidly among susceptible cloven-hoofed animals through direct contact, contaminated materials and movement of animals or animal products. Local veterinary and official animal-health guidance should be followed immediately when this disease is suspected.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether immediate veterinary assessment and official animal-health reporting are required
Ask what information to collect about affected animals, onset dates and herd contacts
Ask what isolation and movement-control precautions are appropriate while awaiting professional guidance
Ask whether other animals on the premises or recent contacts need urgent evaluation
urgent_flags: Mouth, foot, teat or muzzle blisters or erosions
Multiple animals affected or rapid herd spread
Severe lameness, drooling or inability to feed
Fever, marked dullness or sudden drop in milk production
Recent animal movement, market exposure or contact with affected herds
Young animals weak, collapsed or suddenly dead

overview: The image is visually closest to the fungal-infection-in-dog class. Fungal skin disease can resemble allergy, parasites, bacterial skin disease or self-trauma, and different fungal causes require different diagnostic approaches. This card is educational; veterinary testing is needed before using the image label as a confirmed cause.
typical_signs: Circular or patchy hair loss
Scaling, dandruff-like flakes or crusting
Redness or inflamed skin
Broken hairs or rough coat in the affected area
Variable itching, from absent to intense
One lesion or multiple spreading lesions
Lesions may involve the face, feet, trunk or other contact areas
transmission: Some fungal skin infections, especially dermatophyte-type disease, can spread between animals and people. Other fungal or inflammatory mimics may not be contagious, so veterinary confirmation and household risk assessment matter.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether fungal culture, microscopy, lamp examination or other testing is needed
Ask whether allergy, mites, bacterial infection or self-trauma should also be ruled out
Ask whether other animals or exposed people should be considered if lesions are spreading
Ask what handling and environmental precautions are appropriate while waiting for confirmation
urgent_flags: Rapid spread or many lesions
Young, elderly or immunocompromised people exposed
Multiple animals in the household developing skin signs
Open sores, pus, bad odor or severe inflammation
Poor general condition, fever or reduced appetite
Lesions near the eye or extensive facial involvement

overview: The image is visually closest to the hot-spots-in-dog class, also called acute moist dermatitis in many veterinary references. Hot spots are rapidly inflamed, moist skin areas that can follow itching, moisture, allergy, parasites, ear disease or self-trauma. A photo can identify a compatible appearance but cannot determine the trigger or whether deeper infection is present.
typical_signs: Moist red patch of skin
Hair loss or matted hair over the area
Licking, chewing, rubbing or scratching
Pain or sensitivity when touched
Rapid enlargement over hours to days
Surface discharge, crusting or odor
Commonly noticed on the head, neck, hips or limbs
transmission: Hot spots themselves are usually a reaction pattern rather than a contagious disease label. The underlying trigger can vary, and parasites or infection can coexist, so spread to other animals should be discussed with a veterinarian.
ask_your_vet: Ask what underlying trigger should be checked, such as allergy, parasites, moisture or ear disease
Ask whether the lesion needs in-person examination or diagnostic evaluation
Ask what signs suggest deeper infection or pain
Ask whether recurrent hot spots indicate a broader skin or ear problem
urgent_flags: Rapid expansion or large painful area
Pus, bad odor, heavy discharge or open skin
Severe pain, agitation or inability to rest
Fever, lethargy, poor appetite or weakness
Lesion near the eye, ear canal, genitals or feet
Repeated episodes or multiple lesions at once

overview: This cattle label means the image is visually closest to lumpy-skin-disease examples in the dataset. Lumpy skin disease is a serious cattle disease associated with nodular skin lesions and herd-level implications, while some abscesses, insect bites, papillomas or other nodular diseases can mimic it. Suspected cases should be reviewed through veterinary and official animal-health channels.
typical_signs: Firm raised skin nodules
Nodules over the head, neck, trunk, udder or limbs
Swelling of limbs, dewlap or lymph-node regions
Fever, dullness or reduced appetite
Reduced milk production or weight loss
Eye or nasal discharge in some animals
Multiple animals affected within a herd or area
transmission: Lumpy skin disease can spread within and between cattle populations, with biting insects and animal movement playing important roles. Because of herd-health and regulatory implications, suspected cases should follow local veterinary and animal-health-authority guidance.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether herd-level examination and official reporting are required
Ask what history to collect, including onset, animal movements, insect exposure and affected herd size
Ask whether other cattle on the premises should be examined
Ask what isolation or movement-control precautions are appropriate while awaiting guidance
urgent_flags: Many firm nodules or rapidly increasing numbers of lesions
Fever, marked weakness or reduced feeding
Multiple cattle affected or rapid herd spread
Swelling of limbs, face, udder or lymph-node regions
Eye involvement, nasal discharge or breathing difficulty
Recent movement from or contact with affected areas

overview: The image is visually closest to the mange-in-dog label. Mange is a broad term for mite-associated skin disease, and image appearance cannot distinguish mite species or separate mites from allergy, infection or fungal disease. Veterinary skin examination and mite-directed diagnostics may be needed, especially when itching is severe or multiple animals are affected.
typical_signs: Hair loss, often patchy or spreading
Crusting, scaling or thickened skin
Redness and irritation
Itching that may be intense in some forms
Scratches, scabs or self-trauma
Lesions on ears, elbows, hocks, face, belly or trunk
Secondary odor or discharge if skin is damaged
transmission: Some forms of mange are contagious between animals and can cause temporary irritation in people, while other mite-related conditions are less contagious. The distinction cannot be made from the uploaded image alone.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether skin scraping, tape prep or other parasite testing is needed
Ask whether the pattern is more compatible with contagious mites, allergy, infection or another cause
Ask whether close-contact animals should be examined
Ask what household or kennel risk questions should be considered while awaiting confirmation
urgent_flags: Severe itching, self-injury or inability to rest
Large areas of hair loss, crusting or thickened skin
Weight loss, poor body condition or weakness
Young, elderly, frail or immunocompromised animal affected
Human skin irritation or multiple animals developing signs
Open sores, pus, bad odor, fever or lethargy

overview: The image is visually closest to the normal-cattle-skin class in the training taxonomy. This does not exclude early disease, lesions outside the photographed area, hidden foot or mouth lesions, or herd-level problems. In livestock, the animal's behavior, appetite, milk production, temperature and whether other animals are affected are as important as the image.
typical_signs: No obvious focal lesion in the uploaded view
Skin and hair coat appear broadly even in the photographed area
No visible nodules, circular hair loss, crusting, wounds or discharge
No obvious swelling or lameness visible in the image
Dirt, hair length, lighting and camera distance can hide subtle lesions
transmission: Normal skin is not a transmissible disease label. If several animals show skin lesions, fever, lameness, mouth lesions or reduced production, a herd-health problem may still be present despite a normal-looking single image.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether the photographed area looks normal for this animal and breed
Ask what additional views are useful if lesions are suspected elsewhere
Ask whether temperature, appetite, milk production or herd spread should be checked
Ask whether herd-level review is needed if more than one animal is affected
urgent_flags: Fever, dullness, poor appetite or sudden production drop
Rapid spread of lesions or multiple animals affected
Open wounds, discharge, swelling or painful skin
Lameness, mouth lesions, drooling or reluctance to eat
Many nodules or circular crusting lesions
Recent animal movement or contact with sick animals

overview: The image is visually closest to the ringworm-in-cat label. Ringworm is a dermatophyte fungal skin disease and may look like allergy, mites, bacterial infection or grooming-related hair loss, especially in cats. Veterinary confirmation is important because ringworm can affect other animals and people.
typical_signs: Circular or patchy hair loss
Scaling, flakes or crusts
Broken hairs or rough coat
Lesions on the face, ears, feet or body
Mild, absent or variable itching
Multiple small lesions or spreading areas
Some cats may carry or spread dermatophytes with subtle signs
transmission: Ringworm can be contagious between cats, other animals and people through direct contact or contaminated material. Zoonotic risk is especially important for young children, older adults and immunocompromised people.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether fungal testing is needed to confirm dermatophyte disease
Ask whether other animals in the household should be examined
Ask what household exposure and handling precautions are appropriate while awaiting confirmation
Ask whether human skin lesions after contact should prompt medical advice
urgent_flags: Many lesions or rapid spread
Young, elderly or immunocompromised people exposed
Multiple animals developing similar skin signs
Lesions near the eye or extensive facial involvement
Open sores, pus, bad odor or poor general condition
Shelter, rescue, cattery or multi-animal setting

overview: The image is visually closest to the ringworm-in-dog label. Ringworm is a dermatophyte fungal skin disease, but dogs with allergy, mites, bacterial skin disease or self-trauma can have similar patches of hair loss and scaling. A veterinary test is needed before using the label as a confirmed cause.
typical_signs: Patchy or circular hair loss
Scaling, crusting or broken hairs
Redness around the lesion
Variable itching
Lesions on face, feet, limbs or trunk
One lesion or multiple spreading lesions
Contact history with affected animals or people may be relevant
transmission: Ringworm can be contagious between dogs, cats, other animals and people through direct contact or contaminated material. Household and kennel exposure should be discussed with a veterinarian when this label appears.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether fungal culture, microscopy or other testing is needed
Ask whether allergy, mites or bacterial skin disease should also be ruled out
Ask whether other animals or exposed people should be considered
Ask what handling and environmental precautions are appropriate while awaiting confirmation
urgent_flags: Many lesions or rapid spread
Young, elderly or immunocompromised people exposed
Multiple animals developing similar signs
Open sores, pus, bad odor or severe inflammation
Lesions near the eye or extensive facial involvement
Poor appetite, fever or marked lethargy

overview: The image is visually closest to the ringworm-in-cattle label. Cattle ringworm is a dermatophyte fungal skin disease, but crusting, hair loss and circular lesions can also come from parasites, trauma, bacterial disease or environmental irritation. Veterinary confirmation matters for herd management and zoonotic risk.
typical_signs: Circular patches of hair loss
Gray-white scaling or crusting
Thickened or raised circular plaques
Lesions often around the head, neck, eyes or body
Usually mild itching but variable discomfort
Multiple animals may show similar lesions
Lesions may be more noticeable in young or grouped cattle
transmission: Cattle ringworm can spread between animals and can be zoonotic. Transmission can involve direct contact and contaminated equipment, housing or handling surfaces.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether fungal confirmation is needed
Ask whether other cattle in the group should be examined
Ask what herd-contact and handling precautions are appropriate
Ask whether human skin lesions after cattle contact require medical advice

Human skin lesions after cattle contact
Lesions near the eye or extensive facial involvement
Open wounds, discharge or severe inflammation
Poor body condition, fever or reduced feeding
Young or stressed animals heavily affected

overview: The image is visually closest to the skin-allergy-in-cat label. Allergic or hypersensitivity skin disease can resemble parasites, ringworm, bacterial infection, food-associated disease or overgrooming from other causes. Photos alone cannot identify the trigger, so the value of this label is to guide a structured veterinary workup.
typical_signs: Itching, scratching or rubbing
Overgrooming or barbered hair
Redness or irritated skin
Hair loss on belly, limbs, flank, face or neck
Scabs, small crusts or miliary dermatitis pattern
Ear irritation or recurrent skin flare-ups
Seasonal or recurring pattern in some cats
transmission: Allergy itself is not contagious. However, parasites, ringworm or infection can mimic allergic skin disease and may spread, so contagious causes should be considered when lesions involve several animals or people.
ask_your_vet: Ask what causes should be ruled out before calling the problem allergy
Ask what history details are useful, such as flea exposure, diet, seasonality, indoor-outdoor access and other animals
Ask whether skin, parasite or fungal testing is appropriate
Ask what signs suggest secondary infection or another diagnosis
urgent_flags: Severe itching, self-trauma or inability to rest
Open sores, bleeding, pus or bad odor
Rapid spread or many new lesions
Poor appetite, fever, lethargy or hiding
Facial swelling, eye involvement or ear pain
Multiple animals or people developing skin signs

overview: The image is visually closest to the skin-allergy-in-dog label. Allergic dermatitis in dogs can overlap visually with parasites, bacterial or yeast skin disease, fungal infection, irritant exposure and self-trauma. The image label should be used as a triage cue for a veterinary workup rather than as proof of an allergy trigger.
typical_signs: Itching, licking, chewing or rubbing
Redness, especially around paws, belly, armpits, groin, face or ears
Hair loss or recurrent irritated patches
Ear irritation or recurrent ear debris
Scabs, crusting, scaling or thickened skin
Odor or discharge when secondary infection is present
Seasonal, dietary or environmental pattern in some dogs
transmission: Allergy itself is not contagious. Parasites, ringworm and some infections can mimic or complicate allergy-like skin disease, so household spread or zoonotic concern should be discussed with a veterinarian.
ask_your_vet: Ask what causes should be ruled out before assuming allergy
Ask whether skin cytology, parasite testing, fungal testing or other diagnostics are needed
Ask what history details are useful, such as seasonality, flea exposure, diet, ear signs and contact with other animals
Ask what signs suggest secondary infection or a more urgent problem
urgent_flags: Severe itching, self-injury or inability to sleep
Open sores, bleeding, pus or bad odor
Rapid spread, swelling or extensive redness
Fever, lethargy, poor appetite or weakness
Face, eye, ear canal, paw or genital involvement
Multiple animals or people developing skin signs

overview: The image is visually closest to the tick-infestation-in-dog label. Visible ticks or tick-like dark bodies on the skin can be confused with scabs, debris, small masses or other parasites, so careful inspection is needed. Tick exposure can also raise concern for tick-borne illness, which cannot be judged from the skin photo alone.
typical_signs: Visible attached ticks or small dark bodies on the skin
Local redness, swelling or scab at an attachment site
Scratching, licking or irritation
Multiple parasites or clustered attachments in heavy exposure
Weakness, fever or behavior change when systemic illness is present
Pale gums or bruising-like changes in more concerning cases
History of outdoor, grassy, wooded or livestock-area exposure
transmission: Ticks can transmit pathogens depending on region, tick species and exposure time. The image cannot determine infection risk, so systemic signs or heavy exposure should be reviewed by a veterinarian.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether the animal should be assessed for tick-borne disease risk
Ask what signs require urgent veterinary assessment after tick exposure
Ask whether the finding is truly a tick versus scab, skin mass or another parasite
Ask whether other animals in the household have similar exposure risk
urgent_flags: Weakness, collapse or sudden behavior change
Fever, poor appetite or marked lethargy
Pale gums, bruising-like spots or bleeding
Many ticks or heavy infestation
Lameness, swollen joints or severe pain
Vomiting, difficulty breathing or neurologic signs

overview: This cattle label means the image is visually closest to papilloma-like skin growths in the dataset. Papillomas are wart-like masses, but nodules, tumors, abscesses, scars, insect reactions and other skin diseases can look similar in photos. An in-person examination is important when a growth changes, bleeds, ulcerates or interferes with normal function.
typical_signs: Raised wart-like skin growth
Single or multiple nodules or masses
Rough, cauliflower-like or irregular surface
Surface crusting, rubbing or irritation
Growths on head, neck, udder, teats, limbs or other contact areas
Bleeding or ulceration if traumatized
Interference with walking, feeding, milking or tack/equipment contact
transmission: Some papilloma-like conditions can spread between cattle through contact or contaminated equipment, depending on the cause. Other masses are not contagious, so veterinary assessment is needed for risk classification.
ask_your_vet: Ask whether the growth needs examination, sampling or monitoring
Ask what changes in size, color, bleeding or ulceration are concerning
Ask whether other animals should be checked if multiple cattle have similar growths
Ask whether the location creates risk for pain, trauma, milking difficulty or movement problems
urgent_flags: Rapid growth or sudden change in appearance
Bleeding, ulceration, discharge or bad odor
Pain, swelling or repeated trauma to the growth
Interference with walking, feeding, milking or vision
Many animals affected or rapid appearance of new masses
Fever, weight loss, reduced feeding or poor condition

overview: The image is visually closest to the scabies-cat label, a mange-like mite disease category. Several feline skin diseases can resemble scabies in photos, including ear mites, allergy, ringworm, bacterial infection and overgrooming. Veterinary testing is important because contagious mite disease changes the risk assessment for other animals and people.
typical_signs: Intense itching, scratching or rubbing
Crusting, scaling or thickened skin
Hair loss on ears, face, neck, limbs or body
Redness and self-trauma

Possible spread to other animals in close contact

Ask whether ringworm, allergy, ear mites or bacterial infection should also be ruled out
Ask whether other animals in the household should be examined
Ask whether human skin irritation after contact should prompt medical advice

Rapid spread or many crusted lesions

overview: The image is visually closest to the scabies-cattle label, a mange-like mite disease category. Hair loss, crusting and thickened skin in cattle can also reflect ringworm, lice, allergy, trauma, nutrition-related coat change or bacterial disease. Hair loss, especially in rubbed areas
Crusting, scaling or thickened skin
Redness, wounds or self-trauma from rubbing
Lesions on neck, shoulders, tail head, limbs or body

Ask whether herd-level examination is required
